title: Transit Enforcement and MSA Transport Policing: Security in the Moving City
body:
Transit enforcement in GLMZ is a distributed function divided between the Meridian Security Authority's Transit Division, private security contractors employed by individual transit operators, and the corporate security departments of the franchise holders themselves. The result is a policing architecture with overlapping jurisdictions, inconsistent standards, and a consistent pattern of enforcement intensity that correlates strongly with the citizenship tier of the population being served. Spine Corridor stations in Tier-One zones average one MSA Transit Division officer per 800 passengers during peak hours; stations in Tier-Three zones average one per 4,200 passengers. Sub-street transit infrastructure has no formal MSA Transit Division presence at all.

Fare enforcement is the most visible routine function of transit security personnel, and the disparities in its application are among the most documented and contested aspects of the system. Velorant's proprietary fare-enforcement algorithm — which triggers targeted inspection of individual passengers based on behavioral, biometric, and citizenship-tier data — has been shown in multiple independent analyses to flag Tier-Three and Tier-Four passengers at rates six to eight times higher than Tier-One passengers with equivalent fare compliance rates. Velorant contests these analyses as methodologically flawed. The penalties for fare non-compliance are also tiered: Tier-One passengers receive administrative notices with 30-day payment windows; Tier-Three and Tier-Four passengers face immediate detention pending payment, with failure to pay resulting in citizenship grade demerits that can trigger cascading consequences across housing, employment, and credit access.

Beyond fare enforcement, transit security personnel exercise a range of discretionary powers that effectively function as mobility controls. MSA Transit Division officers have authority to require identity verification from any person in a transit zone, to deny access to transit infrastructure pending verification, and to detain individuals for up to four hours pending citizenship status confirmation. These powers are used with notable frequency against individuals who do not have active neural interfaces — a population that skews heavily toward Tier-Four and unregistered residents. The absence of a real-time-verifiable neural identity signature is treated, in practice, as a basis for enhanced scrutiny regardless of whether the individual possesses valid physical documentation.

Transit security incidents — altercations, detentions, use of force — are logged by MSA but the logs are not publicly available. Worker advocacy groups and unlicensed mesh journalists have assembled partial pictures through witness testimony and leaked incident reports. These accounts describe a pattern of enforcement that functions less as safety provision than as demographic management: keeping lower-tier passengers moving quickly through higher-tier zones, discouraging extended presence, and creating a friction-based deterrent against sub-street and Tier-Four residents using transit infrastructure in ways that make upper-tier users uncomfortable. Several transit operators have explicit contractual provisions with their private security contractors specifying response time targets and 'passenger comfort' metrics that effectively operationalize this function.
